newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's daughter ready to continue mystery role.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's daughter ready to continue mystery role.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana, whose influence has been growing since she helped secure his reelection in July, says she is ready to continue serving her father in whatever role he sees fit.
But Tatyana Dyachenko is keeping Russians guessing about her mysterious role behind the scenes, which ousted Kremlin aides say now gives her immense influence.

"During the election campaign I worked in the campaign team. What will happen now is hard to say -- whatever suits Dad. I'll always work for him in whatever capacity he says," she told NTV commercial television in an interview on Sunday night.
Asked of she would ever refuse a request by her father, she said: "Never."

Her comments in the Central Clinical Hospital where the 65-year-old president is recovering from open heart surgery skirted around the issue of what role she has played since joining the campaign team this spring.

"I wouldn't say I have been involved in politics. Of course there were the elections and Dad asked me to help him, although the family, (Yeltsin's other daughter) Lena and our husbands, always help him," she said.

But the remarks are sure to whet the appetite of Kremlin watchers who say the 36-year-old mother of two has formed a powerful alliance with Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, acting as joint "gatekeepers" while the president has been ill.
Under this scenario, Chubais has the support of powerful financial backers who also helped secure Yeltsin's reelection and still have huge influence.

The roles of Dyachenko, who has no formal post, and Chubais are likely to be scrutinised by Yeltsin as he recovers and prepares to tackle the political and economic problems that have piled up in his absence from the Kremlin.
Some political commentators suggest Yeltsin should drop both to show he is firmly in control and that his daughter is not influencing his decisions or taking them for him.

"Where it is a question of taking decisions, moreover on the level of the president, the participation of relatives in political affairs must be based on clearly written legal norms," the Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper wrote at the weekend.
"If there are no legal grounds for a temporary 'substitution', such forms of drawing close ones and relatives into politics can bring nothing but harm."

As Nezavisimaya Gazeta pointed out, there is no evidence to show Dyachenko has influenced Yeltsin in initiating or signing decrees in the last few weeks -- much of which she has spent at his side because First Lady Naina Yeltsin has also been ill.

But Nikolai Yegorov, Yeltsin's Kremlin chief of staff until July, said in a newspaper interview that Dyachenko had gained in influence between the first round of the presidential election on June 16 and the second round on July 3.
"The only person to whose opinion he listened was his younger daughter Tatyana," Yegorov told Komsomolskaya Pravda.
Another former Kremlin insider, Valery Streletsky, told the daily Moskovsky Komsomolets: "She is the one who influences her father most."
Such comments could be dimissed as griping by disgruntled former aides, and Dyachenko, a stylish dresser with shoulder length auburn hair who manages to look homely, gives little away.

She gives few interviews, hardly appeared in public during the election campaign and her only official appearance was a recent trip to the southern town of Rostov-on-Don to commiserate with the families of children killed in a bus and train crash.
She trained as a mathematician and has two sons, one of whom is called Boris and studies at an exclusive shool in Britain.
Little is known about her private life and, in true Kremlin style, she seems intent on keeping it that way.
